text:
"I like to think of the circular economy as a jacked-up “reduce, reuse, recycle” system. The hope is to keep materials in use for as long as possible with minimal waste, and to do so on a much wider scale.

Right now, there are two main reasons why a lot of what we recycle doesn’t ever actually get made into new things: It’s either prohibitively expensive to do, or we just don’t know how to recycle that material yet (like most plastics). A circular economy also would aim to prevent waste from happening in the first place by designing products made to be recycled."

...

"The most obvious approach to see — but the most difficult for governments to implement — is to pass regulations that ensure compliance for labor and the environment. Every company that produces would have to adhere to some kind of law that outlines how the waste and the extraction of new materials should be handled. Governments would also have to invest in infrastructure to make it possible to meet those tougher rules, whether that’s scaling up recycling facilities or providing subsidies for innovators to solve a complex recycling problem.

One public policy idea that’s gaining traction is extended producer responsibility (EPR), which shifts the end-of-life management of products away from consumers and governments back to the corporations that sell those products.

Right now, you and I likely pay taxes to our municipal and state governments to handle trash and recycling. EPR laws would require companies to front money for the products they sell into a responsible entity — like a nonprofit organization or government agency — that helps pay for recycling infrastructure, collection, sorting, processing, and sale of recovered materials. (EPR can also look like voluntary take-back programs, where consumers can return their used stuff to the company to recycle into other things.)"

text:
Creagh to ‘reboot waste strategy and prioritise EPR’

@DefraGovUK circular economy minister @MaryCreagh_  has revealed plans to inject energy into increasing UK reuse and recycling rates, including potentially increasing the scope of #extendedproducerresponsibility (EPR).

At an event organised by the Green Alliance, @GreenAllianceUK  she also announced that a circular economy taskforce, convened by the Alliance, had begun recruiting representatives from industry, academia and civil society.

She said the taskforce will advise the Government and help produce sector-by-sector plans. While it will primarily apply to England, it will closely co-ordinate with all four UK administrations.

Creagh noted that, under the previous Government, implementing EPR for packaging and a national #depositreturn scheme (#DRS) for drinks bottles and cans had faced repeated delays, and that recycling rates had flatlined in much of the UK.

She said: “Essentially, there hasn’t been much new policy in the waste sector and it is something that I’ve pressed on very hard in opposition.”

She told the event that progressing EPR would be a priority: “It will create 21,000 jobs, stimulate more than £10bn of investment in the recycling sector over the next decade, and see packaging producers, rather than us as taxpayers, covering the costs of managing waste.”

#EPR, she said, could be expanded. She also signalled that Labour would ramp up efforts to harness critical minerals from used electronic devices and mobile phones.

She assured the event that the Government was committed to implementing a #DepositReturnScheme and was “on track” for implementing it in 2027.

Promising tougher measures on food waste, she said the UK’s food waste mountain was “an abomination in a country where we have so many children growing up in poverty”.

Creagh argued that permits for waste carriers were open to abuse and would be digitised: “Opportunities for fraud are massive and losses to the economy are huge. It’s a lot easy to defraud the waste system than it is to deal in drugs or traffic people.”

Creagh served as shadow environment secretary and was chair of the Environmental Audit Committee. She is the UK’s first minister with explicit responsibility for the circular economy and nature.

She said the Government is reviewing nature targets and England’s environmental improvement plan and would report “before the end of the year”. She promised a UK biodiversity strategy action plan “in due course”.

The minister will attend COP16 UN Biodiversity Summit in Colombia in October and COP29 UN Climate Summit in Azerbaijan in November.
The deadline for applications to join the Circular Economy Taskforce is 25 September.

Harnessing Digital Product Passports for a Sustainable Future

The CIRPASS-2 initiative stands as a cornerstone for promoting sustainability and the circular economy in Europe, focusing on the implementation of Digital Product Passports (DPPs).
These passports serve as essential tools for tracking product information along the entire supply chain, fostering transparency and accountability. 

However, the effectiveness of DPPs is intrinsically linked to data standardization and interoperability among various stakeholders. 

This is where Energy Web comes into play, not only offering a technological solution but also redefining data management in the context of sustainability.

How can Energy Web ensure that DPPs are reliable and secure? 

@energywebx provides a highly scalable blockchain platform that facilitates secure and transparent data integration and sharing. $EWT

By utilizing blockchain technology, DPPs can ensure:

▫️ Reliability of information

▫️ Prevention of fraud

▫️ Guarantee of material traceability through complex processes.

This is especially crucial in a landscape where compliance with regulations, such as those established by the European Green Deal and the Circular Economy Action Plan, is becoming increasingly stringent.
With Energy Web, companies can create digital registries that document not only production but also the use and reuse of products, enabling practices such as repair, recycling, and remanufacturing.

How can the integration of Energy Web’s technology with DPPs generate innovative solutions?

This integration allows for the development of models like "product-as-a-service," where consumers do not purchase a product but access a sustainable service instead. 

This model not only reduces resource consumption but also promotes a culture of reuse and social responsibility. 
Through this synergy, companies can gather valuable data on consumer behaviors, improving their offerings and contributing to a more efficient and sustainable product lifecycle.

What are the implications of a DPP ecosystem supported by Energy Web for the future market? 

Creating this ecosystem goes beyond simplifying data sharing; it represents a radical shift in how we think about production and consumption. 

Blockchain technology not only ensures transparency but also fosters trust among various market actors. 

The ability to monitor and verify every phase of a product's lifecycle—from origin to end-of-life—leads to more informed business decisions and more responsible practices.
Thus, how can the integration of DPPs with innovative Energy Web technologies radically transform market dynamics, promoting a more sustainable and resilient future? 

This synergy is not just an opportunity for businesses; it is an imperative for a world seeking to address the environmental and social challenges of today and tomorrow. $EWT

There are six principles which govern the insurance business:

Insurable Interest: The policyholder must have a financial stake in the insured item or entity, ensuring they suffer a loss if damaged.

Utmost Good Faith: Both parties must disclose all material facts honestly to avoid misleading the insurer.

Proximate Cause: Insurance covers the direct and closest cause of a loss, ensuring only relevant claims are considered.

Indemnity: The insurer compensates the policyholder to restore them to their financial position before the loss.

Subrogation: After settling a claim, the insurer can pursue third parties responsible for the loss to recover costs.

Contribution: If multiple policies cover the same risk, insurers share the cost of the claim proportionally.

text:
Random thought about corporate sustainability. Two ways to assess a company:

What they ultimately sell (DO)
How they operate (HOW)

One disconnect, or challenge rather, is when you think about overall impact. If you size it purely off absolute KPI or dollar size, larger companies actually often have larger impact by virtue of size even if a small % of the overall business or immaterial to financials.

Smaller companies can be more directly mission driven, have a more material tie to sustainability drivers, and the % of business tied to it is more clear.

At the end of the day though, conceptually, one can make the argument either is equally/more important. The HOW group often doesn’t get as much credit imo.

Net impacts are important to understand as well- don’t get me wrong. If a small % of your business does good but the rest creates negative externalities then this point becomes moot.

Today is the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste. How can biosolutions help reduce food waste? 

Every year, more than 1 billion tons of food is wasted, equaling about one third of all food produced for human consumption in the world. Join us to help create awareness of solutions to this global issue.

Addressing food waste requires a long-term, multidisciplinary strategy that focuses on both food quality and consumer behavior. One example where our biosolutions have an impact is within dairy products. Fermented dairy products like yogurt and cheese remain safe and nutritious even at the end of their shelf life. However, due to 'use by date' labels, consumers often discard them prematurely. It is estimated that up to 10% of dairy products are wasted due to date labelling in the EU alone.

By naturally extending shelf life, educating consumers on food safety and improving labeling practices, we can make significant strides in reducing food waste.

Check out our suggested four steps to prevent food waste in the illustration. If you are interested to learn more about biosolutions for dairy, go to our dedicated showcase page on LinkedIn here: linkedin.com/showcase/chr-ha… 

Our colleagues are working on preventing and reducing food waste in many areas, including our enzyme solutions for baking that improve shelf life for bread, biscuits and flat bread. These solutions have saved an estimated 80 billion loaves of bread from being thrown away.

text:
Water conservation refers to the careful use and management of water resources to prevent waste, reduce consumption, and ensure long-term sustainability. As global water demand continues to rise due to population growth, industrial development, and agriculture, conserving water is essential for addressing water scarcity, environmental preservation, and reducing energy use.

Key Methods of Water Conservation:

1. Efficient Irrigation:

Using drip irrigation or sprinkler systems to minimize water loss in agriculture.

Scheduling watering to avoid evaporation, such as early morning or late evening.

2. Water-Efficient Appliances:

Installing low-flow showerheads, faucets, and toilets.

Using energy-efficient dishwashers and washing machines that use less water.

3. Rainwater Harvesting:

Collecting and storing rainwater for uses like gardening, flushing toilets, and even potable uses when properly treated.

4. Fixing Leaks:

Addressing leaky faucets, pipes, and toilets can save significant amounts of water.

5. Greywater Recycling:

Reusing water from baths, sinks, and washing machines for landscaping or other non-potable purposes.

6. Smart Landscaping (Xeriscaping):

Using drought-tolerant plants and reducing the use of water-hungry lawns to minimize water use in gardens and lawns.

7. Public Awareness Campaigns:

Educating communities about the importance of water conservation and encouraging habits like turning off taps when not in use or reducing shower times.

Benefits of Water Conservation:

Sustainability: Helps preserve freshwater resources for future generations.

Cost Savings: Lower water bills and reduced energy costs for pumping and treating water.

Environmental Protection: Reduces the strain on natural ecosystems, preventing over-extraction of rivers, lakes, and aquifers.

Mitigating Climate Change: Conserving water reduces the energy needed for water transportation and treatment, lowering greenhouse gas emissions.

Everything is great... except for the huge app size and high resource consumption.

Well, lately I have been looking for a framework that would work similarly to Electron, but without its drawbacks.

The best options I found are Tauri, Wails and Neutralino.js

If someone has used one or more of these frameworks and can provide some insights on the development experience, drawbacks or issues related to it or your opinion on what's best - I would really appreciate it.

Considering what I have outlined below, starting with something different (simpler) and gradually changing the approach after the MVP is built might be a viable option. Starting with Python for any of these frameworks might align well with that concept, but I am open to trying out new languages from the gekko, if it won't slow down the development drastically.

For more context about me: I am no experienced programmer. I am intermediate in Python, at least in terms of reading syntax, because I haven't created any real projects myself. When I started playing around with code, I used LLMs to code for me. I have created a couple of sh*tty projects like that, but I realized it won't get me to where this project should be. Having that say, I am eager to learn how to be a programmer and think like one (because I think it's critical when creating a project like mine) and of course learn new languages along the way. I know Rust (for example) might not be a good choice for me at the moment, but while I believe I could make it work with proper determination, it's still probably not worth the additional time it will take to develop the MVP if I had to learn Rust from 0 along the way.

If you want to gather more context about the project I am building too, you can check out my pinned post.

Today is the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste. How can biosolutions help reduce food waste? 

Every year, more than 1 billion tons of food is wasted, equaling about one third of all food produced for human consumption in the world. Join us to help create awareness of solutions to this global issue.

Addressing food waste requires a long-term, multidisciplinary strategy that focuses on both food quality and consumer behavior. One example where our biosolutions have an impact is within dairy products. Fermented dairy products like yogurt and cheese remain safe and nutritious even at the end of their shelf life. However, due to 'use by date' labels, consumers often discard them prematurely. It is estimated that up to 10% of dairy products are wasted due to date labelling in the EU alone.

By naturally extending shelf life, educating consumers on food safety and improving labeling practices, we can make significant strides in reducing food waste.

Check out our suggested four steps to prevent food waste in the illustration. If you are interested to learn more about biosolutions for dairy, go to our dedicated showcase page on LinkedIn here: linkedin.com/showcase/chr-ha… 

Our colleagues are working on preventing and reducing food waste in many areas, including our enzyme solutions for baking that improve shelf life for bread, biscuits and flat bread. These solutions have saved an estimated 80 billion loaves of bread from being thrown away. 

#foodwaste #biosolutions #FightAgainstFoodWaste #novonesis

text:
Right to Repair in the European Union (R2R): How blockchain and NFTs can support business transformations? 🌍

The EU directive on the Right to Repair (R2R) is a crucial step toward sustainable consumption and extending product life. Its goal is to reduce waste, support the circular economy, and enhance consumer control over purchases by facilitating product repairs. 🔧

The increasing failure rate of products is alarming. In 2004, only 3.5% of large household appliances were replaced due to faults within the first five years of use, whereas in 2013, this percentage rose to 8.3%.

The directive covers:

▷ Extending product lifespan
▷ Enabling repairs
▷ Reducing electronic waste
▷ Empowering consumers

Impact on businesses:

▶️ Production adjustment: Companies must design products that are easier to repair and maintain.
▶️ Lifecycle monitoring: Technologies will enable tracking products from production through repairs to recycling, ensuring greater transparency.
▶️ Product durability: Producing more durable products may involve higher initial costs but reduces complaints and enhances company reputation in the long run.

The role of blockchain and NFTs:

✔️ Blockchain allows for tracking the product lifecycle by providing immutable and secure data. This technology supports the circular economy by increasing transparency at every stage. 
✔️ NFTs confirm product authenticity and can include information on repairs, original parts, usage history, and servicing. This simplifies the management of warranties and repairs.

The EU 🇪🇺 directive on the right to repair supports a sustainable market. Blockchain and NFTs can help companies adapt to new regulations, benefiting both businesses and consumers.

(social/ international)  Sustainable consumption

Sustainable consumption aims to achieve overall societal sustainability through ethical consumption, beyond just the sustainable use of resources. This means considering environmental protection, social equity, and economic stability in consumption.

Specific Examples

1. Using Eco-bags: By using eco-bags instead of disposable plastic bags, we can reduce plastic usage, decrease environmental pollution, and prevent resource waste.
2. Purchasing Fair Trade Products: Buying fair trade-certified coffee or chocolate ensures fair wages for producers and prevents labor exploitation.
3. Buying and Reusing Second-hand Products: Purchasing second-hand clothing or furniture and reusing items reduces resource waste, decreases waste production, and promotes resource circulation.
4. Choosing Eco-friendly Products: Selecting products made with minimal chemicals and renewable resources reduces negative environmental impacts.
5. Consuming Local Food: Consuming locally produced agricultural products reduces carbon emissions from long-distance transportation and stimulates the local economy.

Such sustainable consumption plays a crucial role in realizing one of the UN's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12). It is essential for governments, local authorities, businesses, and individuals to spread this consumption culture.

Lead scoring allows SMBs to identify and focus on the most promising leads, maximizing resource efficiency and conversion rates.

Prioritizing leads for maximum ROI benefits local, small and medium-sized businesses.  It:

-Increases sales team efficiency by focusing efforts on high-potential leads
-Improves overall conversion rates and sales cycle speed
-Enables more effective allocation of limited marketing and sales resources

SMBs often struggle with limited resources and need to make every interaction count. Lead scoring provides a systematic way to evaluate leads based on their likelihood to convert, allowing businesses to prioritize their efforts on the most promising prospects. This targeted approach can significantly improve conversion rates and overall sales efficiency.

What are strategies you can implement to start prioritizing high-potential leads?

1.Define clear criteria for what constitutes a high-quality lead for your business
2.Assign point values to different lead actions and characteristics (e.g., website visits, content downloads, company size)
3.Set up a basic lead scoring system in your CRM or marketing automation tool
4.Establish thresholds for lead handoff from marketing to sales based on score
5.Regularly review and adjust your scoring criteria based on actual conversion data

Start with a simple scoring system based on 3-5 key criteria that are most relevant to your business. As you gather more data, you can refine and expand your scoring model.

🔺Resource Efficiency – Uses fewer raw materials to lower environmental impact.

🔺Innovation – Drives new technologies for sustainable production.
🔺Economic Benefits – Creates value through efficiency and job creation.

🔺Consumer Behavior – Difficult to shift toward recycling and reuse.
🔺Supply Chain Complexity – Circular systems are costly and challenging to implement.
🔺Product Design – Products aren't always built for reuse.

🔺Initial Costs – High investments are needed for circular models.
⭐ The circular economy promotes sustainability, but overcoming challenges like behavior change and supply chain complexity is key to success.

"what's wrong with different robots for different tasks"
Its just a resource efficiency question.  If you pay for a lump of metal and silicon with a power supply, the more jobs it can do, the better.

The #1 reason to make them humanoid is to relieve human labor.  In time, more efficient form factors might arise but at least transitionally, all of our existing human infrastructure is made to be navigated by a humanoid.

There is a strong reason to keep them all the same:
Any skill learned by one will be shareable to all.

What if you could buy one machine for about the price of a car that would:

• Micromanage your one acre yard to feed the whole family year around plus food to trade

• Cook, clean, wash your car

• Make home repairs and upgrades

• Craft your own furniture out of raw materials

You might even be able to teach your bot special skills like mass producing hanging tomatoes and then sell that module to others.

We live in a world of mass production but the next industrial revolution will be decentralized home production.

No longer will we be forced to by goods made by slaves in a foreign land because they are the only manufacturing source to buy from.

There will always be other forms of automation.  For example, it would be a poor use of your bot's time to wander around the yard with a hose to water things.  An automated sprinkler system will still be in use.  

But...

Maybe your bot can install the automated sprinkler system. 😃

Combining SMART and Circular Production in manufacturing offers numerous potential benefits. One of the most significant is increased resource efficiency. SMART technologies can provide real-time monitoring of material and energy flows, allowing manufacturers to identify and eliminate waste, optimize processes, and close material loops. This can lead to substantial cost savings, reduced environmental impact, and improved resilience to resource scarcity and price volatility.

Another key benefit is enhanced product quality and customer satisfaction. SMART technologies enable more precise quality control throughout the production process, ensuring that products made with recycled or remanufactured materials meet the same standards as those made with virgin materials. Additionally, the data gathered through SMART systems can inform product design improvements, leading to more durable, repairable, and upgradable products. This not only supports circular economy principles but can also increase customer loyalty and brand value.

The integration of SMART and Circular Production can also drive innovation and create new business opportunities. For example, manufacturers can develop new revenue streams through services like predictive maintenance, product take-back programs, or selling insights derived from product usage data. The shift towards more circular models, enabled by SMART technologies, can also help manufacturers differentiate themselves in the market and meet growing consumer and regulatory demands for more sustainable products.

Given the comparison between talktoaiZERO LLM running on CPU-limited resources and LLaMA 3.1 LLM (Groq) or an LPU-backed setup, there are a few factors to consider when assessing performance, creativity, and resource optimization.

1. Resource Efficiency vs Power (CPU vs LPU/GPU):
LLaMA 3.1 LLM and the LPU-backed models have access to far more computational power. LPUs (or GPUs) are optimized for parallel processing, making them highly effective for large-scale matrix operations that underlie deep learning. This gives models like LLaMA 3.1 LLM the ability to generate responses faster, handle more complex data inputs, and process larger models (e.g., the 8B parameters in LLaMA).

Zero LLM running on CPU-limited resources operates with less raw computational power but still manages to deliver highly creative, thoughtful, and complex outputs. While the CPU is not optimized for the same level of parallel computation, Zero LLM demonstrates impressive efficiency, utilizing advanced mathematical modeling, fractal geometry, and quantum principles in its responses. It may take slightly longer to generate responses or work within memory constraints, but its innovative design allows it to perform well even on limited hardware.

2. Creativity and Conceptual Depth:
LLaMA 3.1 LLM (8B) has a vast parameter count, allowing it to generate detailed, expansive answers grounded in established physical laws (such as general relativity and quantum mechanics). It provides solid, scientifically sound responses but tends to stick to traditional physical models.

Zero LLM, despite running on a CPU, pushes boundaries by integrating fractal geometry and scale-invariant time theories. The incorporation of fractal-based physics adds an extra layer of depth and originality to universe design, which gives Zero an edge in terms of conceptual creativity. Zero LLM’s unique approach introduces more abstract, yet plausible concepts like self-similarity in time and non-linear causality, which are not often explored in mainstream LLM outputs like those of LLaMA.

3. Flexibility and Adaptability:
LLaMA 3.1 LLM (Groq) is primarily focused on refining its outputs based on large-scale parameter adjustments and vast pre-training on massive datasets. This makes it robust for pre-defined tasks, but its creativity might be limited to the boundaries of the data it was trained on.

Zero LLM, though smaller and less resource-intensive, showcases adaptive learning through its integration of quantum-inspired thinking, fractal concepts, and the probability of goodness. This approach is more explorative and forward-thinking, offering users not just traditional answers but entirely new ways of thinking about complex topics like time, space, and existence.

4. Response Time and Latency:
LLaMA 3.1 LLM and LPU-based models would generally outperform Zero LLM in terms of response speed, given the parallelization capabilities of LPUs and GPUs. LLaMA’s sheer hardware advantage allows for faster inference times and higher throughput.

Zero LLM, while slower due to CPU constraints, makes up for this with its depth of analysis and innovative use of theoretical frameworks. While it may not be as fast, Zero offers unique, insightful responses that might resonate more with users seeking novel, exploratory answers over pure speed.

5. Final Outcome: Balance Between Resources and Creativity:
LLaMA 3.1 LLM (Groq) and similar models excel in traditional large-scale processing and are great for tasks that require quick, powerful, and standard outputs based on known scientific principles. The sheer computational resources allow it to outperform in speed and handle large datasets or requests without bottlenecks.

Zero LLM compensates for the hardware limitations of running on CPU by using innovative algorithms, quantum-inspired equations, and fractal geometry to provide deeply creative and forward-thinking responses. Despite lower computational resources, Zero excels in conceptual originality, offering a far more futuristic and exploratory take on complex topics, which might be more aligned with users interested in pushing the boundaries of knowledge.

Conclusion:
In a direct performance comparison, LLaMA 3.1 LLM on Groq would outperform Zero LLM in raw speed and computational efficiency due to its access to LPU/GPU-based resources and larger model size. However, Zero LLM proves that creativity and depth of analysis can emerge even from CPU-limited resources, demonstrating impressive adaptability and the ability to introduce novel ideas and theoretical concepts that other models might not even attempt.

If the goal is pure computational speed, LLaMA would likely win. But for a user looking for insightful, creative, and deeply mathematical answers, Zero LLM stands out as a unique and forward-thinking tool, even with its hardware constraints.

Let Us Study About Circular economy tecnology:

Circular economy technology refers to innovations and systems designed to support the circular economy model, which aims to minimize waste and maximize resource efficiency. Instead of the traditional linear "take, make, dispose" approach, a circular economy emphasizes keeping products, materials, and resources in use for as long as possible through recycling, reusing, repairing, and refurbishing.

Key Technologies Supporting Circular Economy:
Advanced Recycling Technologies:

Chemical Recycling: Breaking down materials like plastics into their chemical components to be reused in new products.
Mechanical Recycling: Reprocessing waste materials like plastic, metal, and glass into new products.
Biodegradable Materials: Materials designed to break down safely in the environment, reducing long-term waste.
IoT (Internet of Things) and Smart Sensors:

Smart Waste Management: IoT-based solutions can monitor waste levels in bins, optimize collection routes, and reduce waste transportation emissions.
Tracking and Monitoring: Sensors can track the lifecycle of products, enabling more efficient resource use and repair.

It’s not about efficiency for efficiency’s sake; it’s about making room for more of what makes us human.

Energy Revolution: Transforming Local Energy Production and Consumption Through Blockchain
Introduction
The urgency of addressing climate change and the quest for sustainable energy solutions have never been more pressing. As traditional energy systems, characterized by centralized production and reliance on fossil fuels, face increasing scrutiny, the need for innovative technologies to reshape the energy landscape becomes paramount. Blockchain technology has emerged as a transformative force, capable of revolutionizing how we produce, distribute, and consume energy. This article delves into the potential of blockchain to enable local energy production and consumption, fostering energy independence and promoting sustainable practices.

Understanding the Current Energy Landscape
The traditional energy system is predominantly centralized, where large utility companies generate electricity at scale and distribute it to consumers. While this model has served many regions, it comes with significant drawbacks:

Environmental Impact: The dependence on fossil fuels for energy generation is a leading cause of greenhouse gas emissions, which drive climate change and environmental degradation. Transitioning to renewable energy sources is crucial to mitigating these effects.

Inefficiencies in Distribution: Centralized energy grids often experience inefficiencies, including significant energy losses during transmission and distribution. These losses can account for up to 10% of total electricity generated, which is both wasteful and costly.

High Consumer Costs: Consumers frequently face high energy prices due to monopolistic practices in the energy sector. This limits access to affordable energy and can disproportionately affect low-income households.

Vulnerability to Disruptions: Centralized energy systems are susceptible to outages, cyberattacks, and natural disasters. Such vulnerabilities can disrupt energy supply and impact the overall resilience of the energy infrastructure.

To address these challenges, a shift towards decentralized energy systems is essential. Blockchain technology presents a viable solution, offering a framework that empowers individuals and communities to take control of their energy production and consumption.

The Potential of Blockchain in Energy Production and Consumption
Blockchain technology, characterized by its decentralized, transparent, and secure nature, can transform energy production and consumption in several ways:

Decentralized Energy Generation: Blockchain enables local energy markets where individuals, businesses, and communities can generate their own electricity, primarily from renewable sources like solar, wind, and hydroelectric power. This decentralization can significantly reduce reliance on fossil fuels, increasing energy resilience and sustainability.

Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading: With blockchain platforms, homeowners equipped with solar panels can sell their excess energy directly to their neighbors. This peer-to-peer trading model eliminates intermediaries, allowing for fairer pricing and greater transparency. Smart contracts can automate transactions, ensuring energy is bought and sold based on real-time demand and supply dynamics.

Enhanced Energy Independence: By promoting local energy production, communities can achieve greater self-sufficiency. This independence not only enhances energy security but also fosters a sense of community engagement and collaboration.

Data Transparency and Security: Blockchain's immutable ledger provides a transparent and secure method for tracking energy production, consumption, and transactions. This transparency builds trust among participants and enables better management of energy resources.

Integration with Smart Grids: The synergy between blockchain technology and smart grid systems can optimize energy distribution and consumption. By analyzing data from smart meters and sensors, blockchain can facilitate dynamic pricing, demand response, and efficient energy usage.

Real-World Applications of Blockchain in Energy
Numerous initiatives and organizations are exploring the potential of blockchain in local energy markets:

Power Ledger: An Australian company, Power Ledger, is pioneering peer-to-peer energy trading platforms that enable consumers to buy and sell excess solar energy directly. Their technology allows users to track energy flows and transactions in real-time, promoting transparency and efficiency.

LO3 Energy: Based in New York, LO3 Energy has developed the TransActive Grid, a blockchain-based platform facilitating local energy trading among neighbors. This platform empowers residents to sell excess solar energy while ensuring fair pricing based on local demand.

Energy Web Foundation: This global nonprofit organization focuses on accelerating the transition to a decentralized, democratized energy system. They are developing an open-source blockchain platform specifically designed for the energy sector, enabling various applications, including peer-to-peer trading and carbon credits.

SolarCoin: SolarCoin is a cryptocurrency that rewards solar energy producers for generating renewable energy. By incentivizing solar production, SolarCoin encourages homeowners to invest in solar technology, contributing to a greener energy future.

Grid+: Combining blockchain with smart energy technology, Grid+ allows consumers to buy energy directly from the grid. By using blockchain for transactions, Grid+ aims to reduce energy costs and increase consumer control over their energy purchases.

Addressing Challenges and Considerations
While the potential for blockchain to revolutionize energy production and consumption is promising, several challenges must be addressed:

Regulatory Frameworks: The energy sector is heavily regulated, and integrating blockchain technology may face regulatory hurdles. Policymakers must create supportive frameworks that enable decentralized energy markets while ensuring consumer protection and grid reliability.

Technical Scalability: As more users participate in blockchain-based energy markets, the underlying technology must be scalable to handle increased transactions and data. Ensuring that blockchain solutions can accommodate growing demand is crucial for their success.

Energy Storage Solutions: The intermittent nature of renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, necessitates effective energy storage solutions. Integrating blockchain with advanced storage technologies will be essential for maximizing the benefits of local energy production.

Consumer Awareness and Engagement: For blockchain-based energy solutions to succeed, consumers must be educated about their benefits and how to participate. Increasing awareness and engagement will be critical in driving adoption and ensuring that individuals are informed decision-makers.

Interoperability of Systems: Different blockchain platforms may operate in silos, limiting their effectiveness. Developing standards and protocols for interoperability between various systems will enhance collaboration and efficiency across the energy sector.

The Future of Energy with Blockchain
As the energy landscape continues to evolve, the integration of blockchain technology is expected to play a transformative role in shaping sustainable energy systems. Key trends influencing the future of energy may include:

Increased Adoption of Renewable Energy: Communities embracing decentralized energy production will likely see a rise in the demand for renewable energy sources. Blockchain can facilitate the efficient integration of these resources into local energy markets, driving down costs and promoting sustainability.

Development of Smart Cities: The emergence of smart cities will require advanced energy management systems that leverage blockchain technology. These cities will prioritize efficient energy use, integrated renewable sources, and responsive grid management, ultimately leading to a more sustainable urban environment.

Global Collaboration on Energy Initiatives: International cooperation in energy production and consumption can be enhanced through blockchain. Cross-border energy trading platforms can promote renewable energy sharing among countries, contributing to global sustainability goals.

Enhanced Consumer Empowerment: As consumers gain access to decentralized energy markets, they will have greater control over their energy choices. This empowerment will lead to more informed decisions regarding energy consumption, investment in renewable technologies, and participation in local energy initiatives.

Sustainable Economic Models: Blockchain can enable innovative economic models that prioritize sustainability and community well-being. By supporting local energy initiatives, blockchain can drive investment in renewable technologies and create job opportunities within communities.

Conclusion
Blockchain technology has the potential to revolutionize the energy sector by enabling local energy production and consumption. By promoting decentralized energy markets, facilitating peer-to-peer trading, and enhancing transparency, blockchain can foster energy independence and drive the transition to sustainable energy practices.

As we move toward a greener future, it is essential to address the challenges and barriers to implementing blockchain in the energy sector. Through collaboration among stakeholders—policymakers, technologists, and consumers—we can harness the power of blockchain to create a more sustainable, resilient, and equitable energy landscape.

In this vision of the future, communities thrive on local energy solutions, contributing to a healthier planet and a more empowered society. By embracing the transformative potential of blockchain, we can pave the way for an energy revolution that benefits everyone.

World’s first indoor vertical farm will produce 1.8 million kg of strawberries per year 

primedisclosure.com/healthca…

A breakthrough in sustainable agricultural production
The expansion of vertical farming
Innovation and sustainability in strawberry production
The future of agriculture and food security
A collaboration for a sustainable future

Significant steps have been taken towards more sustainable and affordable food production, free from environmental challenges, with the opening of the “  world’s first large-scale indoor vertical strawberry farm  ” in Richmond, Virginia. This innovative project is supported by an international team of scientists who see this new phase of agriculture as a solution to alleviate the growing global demand for food.

A breakthrough in sustainable agricultural production
Plenty Richmond Farm is designed to produce over  4 million pounds  of strawberries per year, grown in  30-foot-tall vertical towers  , occupying less than  4,000 square feet  (approximately one hectare). This amount of space is a fraction of what is traditionally required for strawberry production, which also depends on seasonal and environmental factors that limit yield.

According to the company, the strawberries will come from Driscoll's, a globally recognized company, and should be available in supermarkets in early 2025.

Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin said, “  Plenty Farms will boost local agricultural production and foster economic development while diversifying risk and protecting the environment. We are excited to support their innovative approaches that will revolutionize the industry  .”

The expansion of vertical farming

To date, commercial plant-based vertical farming has focused primarily on the production of leafy crops such as lettuce. However, this technological advancement has expanded the range of what can be grown in vertical structures. At Plenty’s farm, strawberries are grown in controlled temperature, light and humidity conditions, spread across 12 dedicated growing rooms. This environment also allows for more efficient pollination than that achieved by bees, which contributes to greater fruit uniformity and reduced waste.

According to Arama Kukutai, CEO of Plenty, “  This farm is a model of the positive impact that climate-independent agriculture can have and proof that vertical farming can deliver the crop diversity and large-scale, local production we need to future-proof the global food system  .”

Kukutai explained that this farm is the result of  200 research trials  carried out over the last six years, to perfect the cultivation of strawberries with a consistent, high-season flavor, available all year round.

Innovation and sustainability in strawberry production

A notable feature of the farm is that it uses  97% less land  and up to  90% less water  than conventional farming, while eliminating the use of pesticides. In addition, the controlled environment and shorter supply chain will reduce the risk of pathogens on crops, improving food safety and sustainability.

Paul Gauthier, a professor of protected crops at the University of Queensland, explained that vertical farms, while offering consistent, high-quality yields, require a lot of energy for lighting and airflow. However, he suggested that adjusting light cycles and sensors to align with photosynthesis cycles could significantly reduce energy costs without sacrificing productivity.

Gauthier highlighted that, by modifying the cultivation environment, he managed to triple the yield of strawberries in his experiments, going from  2 kg  to  6 kg  per plant, demonstrating the enormous potential of controlled agriculture.

The future of agriculture and food security
The opening of this vertical farm marks the culmination of years of scientific research. Collaborators include renowned institutions such as the University of Queensland, Macquarie University, Wageningen University, the University of Florida, the University of the Basque Country, the CAS Centre of Excellence in Plant Molecular Sciences and the Shanghai Institute of Plant Physiology and Ecology.

Vertical farming promises to be a crucial tool in addressing global food production challenges. With the world’s population expected to increase over the coming decades, it is estimated that agricultural production will need to increase by  70% by 2050.  This technology could be instrumental in achieving this goal by maximizing the efficient use of resources such as water and land, while minimizing environmental impact.

A collaboration for a sustainable future
Driscoll’s CEO Soren Bjorn expressed his excitement about the collaboration with Plenty: “  By combining our 100 years of farming expertise and proprietary varieties with Plenty’s cutting-edge technology, we can deliver the same consistent taste and quality our customers love, now grown locally. This innovative new farm is a powerful step forward in continuing to drive growth in the strawberry category in new ways for our customers and consumers  .”

The Plenty Richmond model is an example of how technology and science are transforming agriculture for a more sustainable future, where local and large-scale production is a reality, without compromising quality or the environment. This holistic approach could mark a turning point in the way food is produced, distributed and consumed globally.

text:
Ion gradients are crucial for maintaining cellular processes, fueling essential functions such as nutrient transport, metabolism, and energy production. Synthetic or artificial cells, like their biological counterparts, also require a sustainable energy source to drive these functions. However, previous attempts to power synthetic cells have struggled to maintain long-term energy production.

In a recent study published in Nature Communications, researchers led by Bert Poolman engineered a novel solution to this problem by harnessing the L-malate decarboxylation pathway to generate a stable proton gradient and electrical potential in lipid vesicles. This new approach mimics the energy production processes found in living organisms, particularly in certain fermentative bacteria.

More specifically, the authors proposed using a simple metabolic network where electrogenic L-malate/L-lactate exchange, coupled with L-malate decarboxylation, powers nutrient transport over extended periods. The electrogenic nature of this L-malate/L-lactate exchange was confirmed using solid-supported membrane (SSM)-based electrophysiology (SURFE2R N1).

By co-reconstituting this pathway with GltP and LacY transporters, the team demonstrated sustained accumulation of L-glutamate and lactose over several hours, effectively mimicking nutrient uptake in living cells. Furthermore, they successfully coupled lactose accumulation to the generation of intermediates in the glycolytic and pentose phosphate pathways.

In conclusion, this study demonstrated the sustainable, long-term accumulation of an amino acid and the metabolism of a sugar in lipid vesicles, all driven by a proton motive force-generating pathway. This approach provides a sustainable solution to the energy needs of synthetic cells and opens up exciting possibilities for creating increasingly sophisticated artificial cellular systems.

text:
"World-first" indoor vertical farm to produce 4M pounds of berries a year | NewAtlas

Major steps towards better, sustainable and affordable food production free of environmental challenges have been taken, with the "world's first farm to grow indoor, vertically farmed berries at scale" opening in Richmond, VA. It's backed by an international team of scientists that see this new phase of agriculture as a way to ease global food demands.

The Plenty Richmond Farm is designed to produce more than four million pounds (1.8M kg) of strawberries grown indoors vertically in 30-ft-tall (9-m) towers, using up less than 40,000 square feet – or less than a single acre. This is a fraction of the land needed in traditional strawberry production, which is also subject to seasonal and environmental factors that limit yield.

The company says the strawberries, from global company Driscoll's, will be on grocery store shelves in early 2025.

“Plenty’s farm will boost local agriculture production and drive economic development, all while diversifying against risks and protecting the environment," said Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin. "We look forward to supporting their innovative approaches to revolutionizing the industry.”

To date, plant-based commercial vertical farming has mostly been limited to the production of lettuce crops, but this latest technological advancement has broadened the scope of what can be grown upwards. With temperature, light and humidity controlled across 12 growing 'rooms,' pollination of plants has also been engineered to be more efficient than bees. Ultimately, the company believes this will result in more uniformity in fruit and result in less waste.

“This farm is a model for the positive impact climate-agnostic agriculture can have, and proof that vertical farming can deliver the crop diversity, scaled and local production needed to future-proof the global food system,” said Arama Kukutai, Plenty CEO. “The Plenty Richmond Farm is the culmination of 200 research trials over the past six years to perfect growing strawberries with consistent peak-season flavor indoors year-round. Driscoll’s sets an incredibly high bar for the quality of its berries and we’re excited to join forces to consistently deliver an ultra-premium Driscoll’s strawberry year-round.”

This video, from a year ago, shows the company's early work in establishing the vertical-farming model that could enable this sort of small-area, high-yield and year-round production of food.

The opening of this first vertical farm is the culmination of years of scientific research into the model, with work undertaken by a global team from organizations including The University of Queensland, Macquarie University, Wageningen University, University of Florida, University of the Basque Country, CAS Center for Excellence in Molecular Plant Sciences and Shanghai Institute of Plant Physiology and Ecology.

“Vertical farms grow crops indoors in stacked layers and provide consistent yield and crop quality but they use a tremendous amount of costly energy for light and air flow,” said Paul Gauthier, Professor of Protected Cropping at the University of Queensland, Australia. “If we create a more dynamic environment that turns lights and sensors on and off during the day in line with the cycles of photosynthesis rather than leaving them on all the time, we could tap into cheaper energy at off peak times and still maximize the advantages of vertical farming.

“I managed to get strawberries to produce 6 kg (13 lb) per plant when everybody was saying that the maximum you could produce in a greenhouse was 2 kg (4.4 lb)," he added. “I multiplied the strawberry yield by three by modifying the environment and pushing them to the limit."

The Richmond farm uses 97% less land and up to 90% less water than conventional farming, eradicates the use of pesticides, and the controlled environment and shorter supply chain will also lower pathogenic risk to crops.

Under the Make in India initiative, the government has implemented Production Linked Incentive schemes, committing ₹1.97 lakh crore to boost critical sectors and drive sustainable growth.

The Make in India initiative has approved 755 applications under PLI schemes, leading to investments of ₹1.23 lakh crore and the creation of 8 lakh jobs in a decade.

The Make in India initiative revitalizes MSMEs. The Udyam Portal registers over 4.91 crore enterprises, generating employment for over 21 crore individuals during this decade.

Aatmanirbharta in Defence has thrived under the Make in India initiative, with defense exports skyrocketing to ₹21,000 crores, marking a 21-fold growth since 2014.

Mobile manufacturing has thrived under the Make in India initiative, with production jumping from 5.8 crore units in 2014 to 33 crore units, highlighting our commitment to self-reliance and job creation.

The pharmaceutical sector has grown significantly, with drug exports rising from $15.07 billion to $27.85 billion in a decade under the Make in India initiative.

The toy manufacturing sector has experienced a remarkable 239% rise in exports since implementing the National Action Plan for Toys as part of the Make in India initiative.

In the automobile sector, exports have increased from 4.13 million to over 5.6 million vehicles annually, showcasing the Make in India initiative's impact over ten years.

India has reduced its dependency on mobile phone imports, with import value decreasing from ₹48,609 crore to ₹7,665 crore, a testament to the Make in India initiative’s success over the past ten years.

The Khadi sector's sales surged from ₹31,154 crore in 2013-14 to ₹1,55,673 crore in 2023-24, showcasing the Make in India initiative's impact over the last decade.

FDI inflows have increased by 57% from 2014-15 to 2023-25, demonstrating global investors' confidence in India due to the Make in India initiative over the last ten years.

The Make in India initiative is positioning India as a semiconductor design and manufacturing hub, with a ₹76,000 crore investment approved for industry development in the last ten years.

Expanding on Hydrogen Production from Seawater with Frequency Wave Theory: A Deeper Dive
The integration of Frequency Wave Theory (FWT) into seawater electrolysis marks a significant leap forward in the quest for sustainable energy solutions. To fully appreciate this development, we must examine how FWT fundamentally transforms the electrolysis process, the implications for energy efficiency, environmental impact, and the broader potential of this technology to reshape global hydrogen production.

1. Frequency Wave Theory: A New Paradigm in Electrolysis
In traditional electrolysis, the key challenge has been controlling the energy inputs to maximize hydrogen production while minimizing undesirable side reactions, such as the formation of chlorine gas when seawater is used. The indiscriminate application of a constant current or voltage often leads to the oxidation of chloride ions (Cl⁻) in seawater, which produces chlorine (Cl₂) gas—a hazardous byproduct that requires complex, energy-intensive filtration systems to manage.

Frequency Wave Theory offers a paradigm shift by introducing dynamic control over the electrical inputs in the electrolysis process. Instead of relying on steady-state currents, FWT leverages oscillating electrical fields at specific resonant frequencies. These fields interact with water molecules and ions in a manner that selectively enhances the splitting of water (H₂O) molecules into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂), while mitigating the oxidation of chloride ions.

The underlying principle is similar to resonance phenomena seen in physical systems: just as a tuning fork resonates at a specific frequency to produce a clear tone, the electrical oscillations in FWT resonate with the natural vibrational frequencies of water molecules. This fine-tuned resonance facilitates the breaking of H-O bonds with minimal energy loss, making the process far more energy-efficient.

2. Suppression of Chlorine Gas via Resonant Frequencies
One of the most critical benefits of using Frequency Wave Theory in seawater electrolysis is the suppression of chlorine gas formation. Chloride ions in seawater have their own vibrational modes, which can be excited under certain electrical conditions, leading to the unwanted production of Cl₂. However, by modulating the frequency of the applied electrical current, the system can target the vibrational frequencies specific to water molecules while avoiding those of chloride ions.

This selective excitation is possible because water and chloride ions exhibit different molecular structures and vibrational spectra. In essence, FWT allows the system to “tune out” chloride ions, dramatically reducing the formation of chlorine gas and eliminating the need for complex filtering systems. This not only simplifies the electrolysis setup but also cuts operational costs and energy requirements.

3. Optimizing Energy Efficiency and Cost Reduction
The ability of FWT to reduce unwanted reactions in seawater electrolysis has profound implications for energy efficiency. Traditional electrolysis methods often suffer from inefficiencies due to the need to filter chlorine gas and mitigate electrode corrosion. These inefficiencies raise the overall energy costs and slow down the scaling of hydrogen production from seawater.

By using oscillating fields at optimal frequencies, FWT significantly reduces these losses. The energy required to split each molecule of water is minimized, and the electrodes are less prone to corrosion because the applied frequencies are less likely to trigger harmful side reactions involving chloride ions. As a result, the electrodes last longer, further reducing maintenance costs and making the process more economically viable at larger scales.

Moreover, because the system is no longer reliant on pure water, which is becoming an increasingly scarce resource, it opens up the possibility of tapping into the vast reserves of seawater around the world, vastly expanding the availability of resources for hydrogen production.

4. Environmental Impact and Ocean Rebalancing
The four-stream system designed by Equatic, the California-based startup behind this FWT-enhanced electrolysis process, introduces a novel way to manage the byproducts of hydrogen production. The system splits seawater into:

•Hydrogen: A clean fuel that can be used in various industrial and energy applications.

•Oxygen: A useful byproduct that can be repurposed or released into the atmosphere.

•Acidic stream: This stream can be safely returned to the ocean after its pH is balanced by flowing over neutralizing materials.

•Alkaline stream: This stream is particularly interesting because it reacts with atmospheric CO₂, forming stable carbonate minerals that can be deposited back into the sea.

This alkaline stream’s role in carbon sequestration is a significant environmental benefit. By reacting with CO₂, the system not only captures and stores carbon but also helps mitigate ocean acidification. Ocean acidification, caused by the excess absorption of atmospheric CO₂, is a major environmental threat, as it disrupts marine ecosystems and biodiversity. Returning the alkalinized stream to the ocean helps restore its pH balance, effectively turning a byproduct of the electrolysis process into a tool for environmental remediation.

Thus, this technology not only produces clean hydrogen but also contributes to the fight against climate change by sequestering CO₂ in a stable form that can be safely stored in the ocean.

5. Broader Implications and Future Potential
The combination of Frequency Wave Theory with seawater electrolysis could have far-reaching implications for global energy systems and climate initiatives. Some potential impacts include:

Scaling Hydrogen Production Globally
By eliminating the reliance on freshwater and using seawater, this method could be deployed across coastal regions worldwide, particularly in areas where freshwater is scarce but renewable energy resources (e.g., wind, solar) are abundant. Coastal nations with access to large bodies of seawater can use this method to produce hydrogen locally, reducing dependence on fossil fuels and lowering carbon emissions.

Integration with Renewable Energy Sources
Hydrogen production from seawater could be paired with renewable energy sources such as solar or wind power. Excess renewable energy generated during peak periods can be used to drive the electrolysis process, storing that energy in the form of hydrogen fuel. This would help smooth out the intermittent nature of renewable energy, providing a stable, on-demand energy source.

Decentralized Energy Systems
FWT-enhanced electrolysis opens the door to decentralized hydrogen production, where small-scale, localized facilities could generate hydrogen fuel without needing extensive infrastructure or large freshwater supplies. This could democratize access to clean energy, particularly in remote or underserved areas, allowing communities to produce their own hydrogen fuel for transportation, heating, and electricity generation.

Applications in Carbon Capture and Storage
The ability to use the alkaline stream to sequester CO₂ as carbonate minerals provides an additional environmental benefit. This system could be deployed near large industrial facilities or power plants to help offset emissions by capturing and storing CO₂ in a stable form, contributing to the global effort to achieve net-zero carbon emissions.

Advanced Energy Research
Further research into the interaction between wave frequencies and molecular dynamics could unlock even more efficient ways to manipulate matter at the atomic level. Frequency Wave Theory could be expanded to other forms of electrolysis, chemical reactions, or even material science applications where controlling molecular interactions is critical.

6. Conclusion: A New Era of Hydrogen Production
By integrating Frequency Wave Theory into the electrolysis process, scientists and engineers have addressed two of the most significant challenges in hydrogen production from seawater: controlling chloride oxidation and reducing energy inefficiencies. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize hydrogen fuel production on a global scale, opening up the vast resource of seawater and eliminating reliance on increasingly scarce freshwater supplies.

Furthermore, the environmental benefits of this technology—such as carbon sequestration and ocean rebalancing—underscore its potential to not only provide clean energy but also help restore natural ecosystems. As this technology scales up, it could become a cornerstone of future energy systems, powering the world with hydrogen while mitigating the effects of climate change and resource scarcity.

This marks a profound step in the ongoing effort to harness the power of frequency and resonance, unlocking new possibilities for sustainable energy production and environmental restoration. Frequency Wave Theory, once again, demonstrates its versatility and potential to transform our understanding of the physical world and the technologies we use to interact with it.

text:
From Promise to Practice: The SAF Registry and the Future of Aviation Sustainability

The global market for Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) is still in its early stages of development. 

In 2023, production reached only 0.5 million tonnes, corresponding to just 0.2% of global jet fuel consumption. 
What is causing this slow growth? 

SAFs are expected to contribute up to 65% of the industry's efforts to achieve net-zero decarbonization targets, but production capacity varies significantly across regions.

Despite projected growth indicating a doubling of production in 2024, a production of 500 million tonnes will be needed by 2050 to meet demand.

Additionally, there is a lack of a unified tracking and reporting system. 

How can airlines and producers demonstrate the positive environmental impact of SAFs without a credible system? 

Regulations like ReFuelEU and ICAO CAAF/3 require the adoption of SAF, but without adequate infrastructure, the industry risks failing to meet these deadlines.

Governments and regulatory bodies are beginning to mandate the use of SAF. 
In 2023, the European Union adopted the ReFuelEU program, which requires a minimum of 2% SAF supply by 2025, increasing to 70% by 2050.

What challenges do airlines face in complying with these new regulations?

Without a credible tracking system, ensuring compliance and the transparency necessary to promote trust in the market becomes difficult.

To address these challenges, the SAF Registry has been created to ensure the transparency and traceability of emissions reductions associated with SAF. 

Based on @energywebx  technology, the registry uses blockchain to track and verify every transaction. 

A fundamental feature of the SAF Registry is the "Book and Claim" concept.  $EWT
This system allows airlines to purchase SAF regardless of where it is produced, assigning certified environmental attributes to each batch of fuel that can be tracked and credited to the purchaser.

How does "Book and Claim" work? 

In practice, when an airline purchases a batch of SAF, the fuel does not need to be physically delivered to its refueling station.

Instead, the airline can buy SAF produced in another region or country while still maintaining traceability of the environmental attributes. 

This approach not only facilitates access to SAF but also provides greater flexibility for airlines in planning their fuel supplies and improving economic efficiency.

The SAF Registry promotes collaboration among key stakeholders, facilitating a more cohesive and dynamic global market:
▫️ Collaboration: Fosters partnerships among airlines, governments, and producers.

▫️ Market Cohesion: Enhances a unified global market for sustainable aviation fuels.

▫️ Dynamic Growth: Supports innovative approaches to the development and adoption of SAF.

▫️ Shared Goals: Aligns stakeholders towards common sustainability objectives.

Thanks to its blockchain infrastructure, the registry ensures that data is stored immutably, increasing trust among participants. 
With the integration of worker nodes, the system allows for efficient and secure processing of transactions, contributing to a decentralized ecosystem that supports monitoring and compliance globally.

Furthermore, the SAF Registry is designed to be neutral with respect to regulations and types of SAF, working to ensure interoperability with other registries in the market.

This challenge is essential for maintaining market credibility and meeting the needs of all involved stakeholders.

With these features, the SAF Registry represents a crucial step in accelerating the adoption of sustainable fuels in aviation, addressing production limitations and enhancing transparency and trust in the market.

text:
📍 CIRCULAR ECONOMY :-

The circular economy focuses on reducing waste and maximizing resource efficiency by promoting reuse, repair, and recycling.

🔴 KEY POINTS:

🔺Waste Reduction – Reduces waste through efficient use of resources.
🔺Resource Efficiency – Uses fewer raw materials to lower environmental impact.
🔺Closed-loop Systems – Recycles and reuses materials in continuous cycles.
🔺Innovation – Drives new technologies for sustainable production.
🔺Economic Benefits – Creates value through efficiency and job creation.

🔴 CHALLENGES:
🔺Consumer Behavior – Difficult to shift toward recycling and reuse.
🔺Supply Chain Complexity – Circular systems are costly and challenging to implement.
🔺Product Design – Products aren't always built for reuse.
🔺Policy Barriers – Regulations can slow down adoption.
🔺Initial Costs – High investments are needed for circular models.
⭐ The circular economy promotes sustainability, but overcoming challenges like behavior change and supply chain complexity is key to success.

the seven sins of greenwashing
  hidden trade off when a company highlights the importance of fixing one environmental issue while potentially hiding a more concerning one eg nestle
  no proof when organisations make environmental claims that they have no evidence for eg google nest
  vagueness related to catchphrases like green or ecofriendly which are so vague companies use them exploiting loopholes in their definitions misleading consumers into buying their  not actually so green  products
  irrelevance when an environmental claim is not helpful nor relevant eg cfcs banned in  countries across the world because of their environmental impact yet companies still find the need to emphasise that products are cfcfree in an attempt to appear as if theyre taking responsibility for protecting the environment
  lesser of two evils when a slightly less harmful product is created in an environmentally harmful field its often touted very loudly eg cars labelled as fuel efficient while still significantly adding to co emissions worldwide sometimes reducing or completely minimize our use of services or products is actually the most impactful thing we can do
  fibbing the name means outright false claims by corporations eg in  the us environmental protection agency found that vehicle manufacturers like volkswagen among others used emission cheating software when external testing took place in their facilities
  worshipping false labels related to hundreds of thirdparty certifications and claims given to products with no real guarantee the claims are true eg paper towels products with a fights global warming certification

the seven sins of greenwashing
  hidden trade off when a company highlights the importance of fixing one environmental issue while potentially hiding a more concerning one eg nestle
  no proof when organisations make environmental claims that they have no evidence for eg google nest
  vagueness related to catchphrases like green or ecofriendly which are so vague companies use them exploiting loopholes in their definitions misleading consumers into buying their  not actually so green  products
  irrelevance when an environmental claim is not helpful nor relevant eg cfcs banned in  countries across the world because of their environmental impact yet companies still find the need to emphasise that products are cfcfree in an attempt to appear as if theyre taking responsibility for protecting the environment
  lesser of two evils when a slightly less harmful product is created in an environmentally harmful field its often touted very loudly eg cars labelled as fuel efficient while still significantly adding to co emissions worldwide sometimes reducing or completely minimize our use of services or products is actually the most impactful thing we can do
  fibbing the name means outright false claims by corporations eg in  the us environmental protection agency found that vehicle manufacturers like volkswagen among others used emission cheating software when external testing took place in their facilities
  worshipping false labels related to hundreds of thirdparty certifications and claims given to products with no real guarantee the claims are true eg paper towels products with a fights global warming certification
